title: Found doing this
hookLine: let death find me attending to my will, Epictetus says (Discourses 3.5)
carry: attending to nothing but my own will

lines: A SICK STUDENT WANTS TO GO HOME.
LET IT BE IN MY OWN BED.
cards: I'm sick here, one of Epictetus' students says, and I want to go home. Not an unreasonable wish: if I'm going to be sick, or worse, let it be in my own bed.
Epictetus answers with questions, and they lead him into a quiet passage of the Discourses, about what any of us would want to be doing when the end comes. It's less grim than it sounds.

teach.h: WOULD YOU BE SAFER AT HOME?
teach.b: This is Discourses book three, chapter five, to students who leave because of illness. Epictetus asks a few practical questions. Would you be in less danger at home?
Is there no fever there? Then he widens the question. Where, and doing what, would you like death to find you?
It's going to find each of us somewhere, doing something: a farmer at his farming, a trader at his trade, an official in office. Epictetus says what he would choose.
Let it find me, he says, attending to nothing but my own will: keeping it calm, unhindered, unforced, free. He wants to be found practicing.
And he imagines being able to say, at the end, that he used well what he'd been given: that he didn't misuse his mind, never complained of his lot, kept his commitments.
That's the heart of the passage, and it isn't really about death. It's about now.
If there's something you'd want to be found doing, you can be doing it already, in ordinary places. Nothing grand. Being patient with the person in front of you.
Doing your work honestly. Treating your own mind with care. His answer is simple enough to carry into a kitchen or an office: whatever I'm doing, let it be something I'd be glad to be found doing.

how: Some Stoic practitioners ask each morning what they would want to be found doing, and use the answer to choose how to spend part of the day.

o: a life with no duties or ties holding it back
free of blocks: a will nothing outside can stop
a body that is healthy and free of illness

games.q: found doing this: tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus tells the sick student he's weak for wanting to go home
he asks practical questions, then widens the question to what we'd want to be found doing.
he says he'd like death to find him attending to his own will
keeping it calm, unhindered, unforced and free.
the passage is mainly about how to plan your death
it's really about living now the way you'd want to be found.

games.q: a student, ill and far from home, wants to leave school. you're Epictetus. what do you ask?
o: where, and doing what, would you like death to find you?
games.why: after a few practical questions, he turns to the larger one, and answers it himself: attending to my will, keeping it free.

practice: This doesn't need to be heavy. Ask yourself, simply: what would I be glad to be found doing?
Let an answer come, being kind, finishing a piece of honest work, laughing with someone, sitting quietly like this, and look for one place in the next few hours where it could fit.

wordCard.voice: Unhindered, one of the four words Epictetus uses for the will he'd want found calm at the end: unhindered, unforced, free. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: attending to nothing but my own will. It's really about now. Day four hundred eighteen.
